//: Realtime Database security rules for Suidoku 1v1. Everything but /rooms is LIVE as published; /rooms (below) is new on 2026-09-30 and must be published by the user.
Paste into Firebase console > Realtime Database > Rules, then Publish.
Kept in the repo so the rules are reviewable and versioned alongside the
transport that depends on them — the console is not a source of truth.
Anonymous auth is enabled (Authentication > Sign-in method > Anonymous),
and the app signs in during firebaseApp.js init. Every read and write
therefore requires auth != null. Without it anyone could fill /queue with
tickets nobody can match, and real players would wait out the full search
against opponents that do not exist — which reads as a broken feature
rather than an attack.
Auth is only half of it. An anonymous account proves a real client asked,
not that it asked for something sensible, so the shape and size checks
below still stand and are still the thing that stops a peer claiming 900%
progress. battleValidation.js checks the same values again on arrival:
the app's check can be bypassed, these cannot.
GOTCHA, learned the hard way: a bare "$other": { ".validate": false } does
NOT mean 'any child other than the named ones'. The wildcard matches EVERY
child, so it rejected playerId/level/timestamp too and every queue write
failed with PERMISSION_DENIED. Each allowed field must be named explicitly
alongside it, which is what the entries below do.
Do NOT relax these to ".read": true, ".write": true — that is an open
database anyone on the internet can wipe or fill.
2026-09-23 (RT-2): ids are now tied to the account that wrote them.
auth != null only proved that SOME client asked. senderId and the queue key
were strings the client chose, so any signed-in client could write a message
as somebody else, and the receiving app believed it — battleValidation's
isFromOpponent compares senderId with the opponent's id, and a peer could
simply repeat that id. Now senderId must equal auth.uid and a ticket must be
written under the writer's own uid, so those strings cannot be borrowed.
Deleting is deliberately asymmetric. A queue ticket must be removable by the
OTHER player, because that is how claiming works (transport/index.js): the
claimer atomically removes the peer's ticket, and exactly one claimer wins.
A bus message is the opposite — its sender owns its cleanup, so only the
sender may remove it, or anyone could delete a match's traffic mid-game.
The app must be shipped before these are published: a client that still
signs with its local id would have every write denied. In the other order
nothing breaks — the new client sends auth.uid either way.
Watch the LENGTHS when an id changes shape. roomId is capped at 64, and the
room id used to be built as room_{peerUid}_{myUid}_{now}. With 28-character
uids that is about 76, so every match_created came back PERMISSION_DENIED:
the host sat in a room the other player never heard of, and that player kept
searching. The id is now short and random (battleMatchmaking.newRoomId).
A refused write shows up as a feature that half works, not as an error.
2026-09-30 (RT-2): /rooms/{roomId}. /bus is readable by every signed-in client,
so every match's progress, rematches and departures were public. A match now
gets its own path: /rooms/{roomId}/members names its two players, written once by
the host, and only a member may read /rooms/{roomId}/msgs or add to it. The
senderId rule is the same as /bus. A member may remove its own membership and
its own messages — nothing else, so nobody can delete a match's traffic.
This section is ADDITIVE. 24 and older never touch /rooms. 25 uses a room only
after a handshake proves both players can read and write it (roomLink.js), and
stays on /bus otherwise — so before these rules are published, 25 behaves exactly
like 24, and a mistake in them sends a match back to /bus instead of breaking it.
Publishing before or after 25 ships are both safe; before means 25-to-25 matches
are private from the first day.

$messageId..write: auth != null && (newData.exists() ? (!data.exists() && newData.child('senderId').val() === auth.uid) : data.child('senderId').val() === auth.uid)

auth != null && (newData.exists() ? (!data.exists() && newData.child('senderId').val() === auth.uid && root.child('rooms').child($roomId).child('members').child(auth.uid).exists()) : data.child('senderId').val() === auth.uid)
